notes.meaning: The Old Testament law was like a rough outline or shadow of the blessings to come, not the real thing itself. Because animal sacrifices had to be repeated every year on the Day of Atonement, they could never completely wash away guilt or make worshippers spiritually complete.

differ.view: Methodists teach that Christian holiness under the gospel can rise much higher than what believers could reach under the old law, because Christ's work provides full sanctification.

notes.meaning: If the old sacrifices had truly removed sin, people would not have needed to keep bringing them year after year. Once worshippers were fully cleansed, their consciences would be free from the burden and fear of God's wrath.

differ.view: Methodists believe that when a person is fully cleansed by grace, they are freed from both the guilt and the inward power of sin.

notes.meaning: Instead of removing sins forever, the yearly Day of Atonement served as an annual reminder of sin. Each year the high priest had to confess the people's failures again, showing that past offerings had not finished the work.

The blood of slain bulls and goats has no real power to wipe out human moral guilt before God. Animal sacrifices only served as a temporary picture pointing forward to the true, living Savior who would offer Himself.

Quoting Psalm 40, the writer shows that God never found final satisfaction in animal offerings, but instead prepared a human body for His Son. Jesus willingly entered the world to obey the Father completely and to fulfill what Scripture had long promised about Him.

Scripture first states that ritual offerings under the law did not truly satisfy God's deepest requirement, and then Christ announces that He has come to do God's will. By doing this, Jesus cancels the old system of animal sacrifices in order to set up His own lasting priesthood.

Because Jesus carried out the Father's plan by offering His own body on the cross, believers are sanctified, or set apart as holy to God. This sacred cleansing was accomplished once for all time and never needs to be done again.

differ.view: Baptists hold that Christ's offering on the cross was finished once for all time, meaning the Lord's Supper is strictly a memorial and not any kind of repeated sacrifice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics teach that the Mass is not an additional or repeated sacrifice, but the very same sacrifice of Calvary made present again in an unbloody manner.

notes.meaning: Old Testament priests had to stand every day at the altar, performing the exact same ceremonies over and over. Their repeated service proved that animal blood could never truly wipe away the guilt of sin.

In contrast to the priests who remained standing, Jesus sat down in the seat of highest honor at God's right hand after offering one single sacrifice for sins. Sitting down signifies that His atoning work is complete, and He now rests with the assurance that all His enemies will eventually be subdued under His feet.

Through that single offering on the cross, Christ has forever completed everything needed to reconcile His people to God. Believers are fully accepted in their standing before God, even as they are continuously being made holy in daily life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics explain that the phrase 'those who are being sanctified' shows salvation is an ongoing process, so the benefits of Christ's sacrifice are continually applied to believers through the sacraments.

notes.meaning: The Holy Spirit confirms this truth through the words of the prophet Jeremiah about the new covenant. In this new arrangement, God writes His laws on the hearts and minds of His people, and He promises never again to hold their sins against them.

Where sins are completely forgiven and blotted out, no more offerings for sin are ever needed. Christ's death settled the debt entirely, so animal rituals and any further sin offerings are finished forever.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics maintain that because Christ won complete forgiveness on the cross, the Church does not offer a new sacrifice for sin, but re-presents the one finished offering of Calvary in the Eucharist.

notes.meaning: Because Jesus shed His blood, believers now have bold, free access to God's presence, the heavenly holy place. Christ opened this fresh, life-giving way through the veil of His human body, and He rules forever as our great Priest over God's household.

Believers are urged to come near to God with an honest, sincere heart and firm trust in Him. Our inner conscience is cleansed from guilt by Christ's blood, and our outward lives are washed and set apart for His service.

Christians must hold tightly to the hope they openly declared when they turned to Christ, without wavering or giving in to doubt. We can be completely confident because God always keeps every promise He makes.

Church members should pay close attention to each other and think about each other's needs. Instead of provoking one another to anger or jealousy, believers are called to stir one another up to love and helpful deeds.

Believers must not stop gathering together for worship and fellowship, as some had begun doing out of fear or spiritual carelessness. Meeting together gives regular opportunity to encourage one another, which becomes more urgent as the day of Christ's return and judgment draws near.

If someone knows the gospel truth and still chooses to deliberately turn away and reject Christ, there is no other sacrifice anywhere that can take away their sins. Renouncing the only Savior leaves a person with nothing to expect except terrifying judgment and God's consuming wrath against His enemies.

differ.view: Reformed Christians believe true believers can never lose their salvation; they understand this passage as a warning that those who commit total apostasy show they were never truly born again.
Methodists teach that genuine Christians who have truly known God's grace can commit deliberate apostasy, making shipwreck of their faith and being eternally lost.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics teach that these verses prove future sins are not automatically forgiven ahead of time, and that a believer who commits mortal sin can forfeit salvation.

notes.meaning: Under the law of Moses, anyone who openly threw off God's covenant and turned to idols was put to death without mercy once two or three witnesses confirmed the crime. God's ancient law demanded strict justice to guard the holiness of His covenant.

Rejecting the gospel is far worse than breaking Moses' law because it treats God's own Son with contempt. An apostate treats Christ's covenant blood as cheap or unholy and deeply insults the Holy Spirit who offers God's free grace.

differ.view: Reformed teachers argue that the phrase 'wherewith he was sanctified' refers either to Christ being set apart, or to an outward, visible dedication in the church rather than inward regeneration.
Methodists teach that the person described was genuinely justified and sanctified by Christ's blood before willfully abandoning the faith.

notes.meaning: God made it clear in Scripture that vengeance belongs strictly to Him and that He will repay wrongdoing. He also warned that He will thoroughly judge His own people, examining the hearts of all who claim to belong to His assembly.

It is a terrifying thing to face the judgment of the living God as an enemy after spurning His mercy. While earthly rulers can only harm the body, the eternal God lives forever and exercises complete and unending justice.

The readers are told to look back on the early days right after they first received the light of Christ. Even when they faced painful hardships, were publicly mocked like actors on a stage, and stood faithfully with other suffering Christians, they did not give up.

These believers showed deep compassion by visiting and helping prisoners, and they even accepted the looting of their own possessions with joy. They could endure earthly loss gladly because they knew they owned a far better, permanent treasure waiting for them in heaven.

Since they had stood firm before, they are urged not to throw away their bold confidence in Christ now like a cowardly soldier discarding his shield. Holding onto faith brings peace now and carries a great, eternal reward from God.

Believers need patient endurance to keep obeying God through ongoing trials and hardships. Only by standing true and doing God's will to the end will we receive the fullness of eternal life that He has promised.

The writer reminds them from the Old Testament that their current trial will last only a little while longer. The Messiah is on His way to rescue His people and bring justice, and He will arrive right on time.

God's righteous people are called to live day by day through steadfast trust in Him. But if anyone cowardly shrinks back from following the Lord out of fear or unbelief, God takes no pleasure in that person.

differ.view: Methodists understand this verse to show that a justified person lives only so long as they retain their faith, and that a believer who draws back can fall into God's displeasure and be lost.

notes.meaning: The chapter finishes with strong confidence that true believers will not turn back into destruction. Instead, they belong to the company of those who remain faithful to Christ and preserve their souls for eternal salvation.
